options.D: Both types of hypervisor can only ever be managed via a physically attached keyboard and monitor, with no remote management option available for either, a restriction that stems from the hypervisor kernel itself lacking any network stack capable of serving a remote management session until a separate management appliance is installed on top of it

questions.explanation_es: Un hypervisor tipo 1 típicamente se gestiona de forma remota (vía un cliente de gestión dedicado, interfaz web, o plataforma centralizada) ya que no tiene un escritorio propio tradicional, mientras que un hypervisor tipo 2 típicamente se gestiona a través de una ventana de aplicación corriendo dentro del propio entorno de escritorio del sistema operativo host.

questions.name: VMs / FT / DRS
questions.question: What is the difference between a 'cold migration' and a 'live migration' (e.g., vMotion) of a virtual machine?

options.A: Live migration can only move a VM to a host running a different hypervisor vendor, while cold migration can only move a VM within the same vendor's hosts
options.B: Cold migration and live migration are two different names for exactly the same process, distinguished only by which time of day the migration is performed
options.C: A cold migration moves a VM between hosts while it is powered off (requiring downtime), while a live migration moves a running VM between hosts with minimal to no perceptible downtime for the workload
options.D: A cold migration is always faster than a live migration, since powered-off VMs transfer instantly with no data movement required at all

questions.explanation_es: Una migración en frío mueve una VM entre hosts mientras está apagada (requiriendo tiempo de inactividad), mientras que una migración en vivo (como vMotion) mueve una VM en ejecución entre hosts con mínima o nula interrupción perceptible para la carga de trabajo.

questions.name: VMs / FT / DRS
questions.question: What prerequisite is typically required for live migration (vMotion) to work between two hypervisor hosts?

options.A: Live migration requires the destination host to be physically located in a different country than the source host
options.B: No prerequisites are needed; live migration can always occur instantly between any two hosts regardless of storage, CPU, or network configuration
options.C: Live migration requires both hosts to be completely powered off during the entire migration process
options.D: The two hosts typically need shared storage accessible to both (so the VM's disk doesn't need to be copied during the migration itself), compatible CPU features (or EVC/compatibility mode), and network connectivity for the migration traffic between hosts

questions.explanation_es: Los dos hosts típicamente necesitan almacenamiento compartido accesible por ambos (para no tener que copiar el disco de la VM durante la migración en sí), características de CPU compatibles (o modo de compatibilidad EVC), y conectividad de red para el tráfico de migración entre hosts.

questions.name: VMs / FT / DRS
questions.question: How does DRS (Distributed Resource Scheduler) decide when to migrate a VM from one host to another within a cluster?

options.A: DRS requires an administrator to manually initiate every single migration; it has no automated decision-making capability of its own
options.B: DRS migrates VMs strictly on a fixed periodic schedule, such as once every 24 hours, configured by the administrator, independent of any real-time CPU or memory utilization thresholds being crossed on a given host
options.C: DRS only migrates a VM once per calendar year, regardless of how unbalanced the cluster's resource utilization becomes
options.D: DRS continuously monitors resource utilization (CPU, memory) across the hosts in a cluster and, based on configured thresholds/aggressiveness settings, recommends or automatically performs live migrations of VMs to balance load and resolve resource contention across the cluster

questions.explanation_es: DRS monitorea continuamente la utilización de recursos (CPU, memoria) en los hosts de un clúster y, según umbrales/nivel de agresividad configurados, recomienda o realiza automáticamente migraciones en vivo de VMs para balancear la carga y resolver contención de recursos en todo el clúster.

questions.name: VMs / FT / DRS
questions.question: What does a 'DRS affinity rule' or 'anti-affinity rule' allow an administrator to configure?

options.A: Affinity and anti-affinity rules only control which color label is displayed next to a VM's name in the management console, with no actual placement effect, a cosmetic feature carried over from an earlier console release that used color-coding before DRS placement logic existed as its own scheduling engine, with the color values simply retained afterward for visual consistency in the UI
options.B: Affinity rules apply only to network switch port configuration and have no relationship to VM placement across hosts
options.C: An affinity rule can require certain VMs to always run on the same host (affinity) or, conversely, an anti-affinity rule can require certain VMs to always run on separate hosts (e.g., keeping redundant application servers apart so a single host failure doesn't take down both instances at once), influencing where DRS places and migrates those VMs
options.D: Anti-affinity rules force every VM in the cluster to run on exactly the same single host at all times, with no distribution across the cluster

questions.explanation_es: Una regla de afinidad puede requerir que ciertas VMs siempre corran en el mismo host (afinidad) o, al contrario, una regla de anti-afinidad puede requerir que ciertas VMs siempre corran en hosts separados (por ejemplo, manteniendo servidores de aplicación redundantes separados para que la falla de un solo host no derribe ambas instancias a la vez), influyendo en dónde DRS coloca y migra esas VMs.

questions.name: VMs / FT / DRS
questions.question: How does VMware HA (High Availability) differ from Fault Tolerance (FT) in how it responds to a host failure?

options.A: HA and FT can never be enabled on the same cluster simultaneously under any vendor's licensing model
options.B: HA relies on a continuously synchronized lockstep secondary VM to avoid any downtime during a host failure, while FT simply restarts the affected VMs on another surviving host after detecting the failure, resulting in a brief interruption and a full OS and application restart
options.C: HA detects a host failure and then restarts the affected VMs on other surviving hosts in the cluster (involving a brief downtime and a full OS/application restart), whereas FT keeps a live, continuously synchronized secondary copy of a protected VM running in lockstep on another host, allowing an instantaneous takeover with no restart and no loss of in-memory state
options.D: HA and FT both maintain a continuously running secondary VM instance kept in lockstep with the primary, differing only in that HA restarts the secondary's guest OS after a failover while FT resumes the secondary instantly without any restart

questions.explanation_es: HA detecta la falla de un host y luego reinicia las VMs afectadas en otros hosts sobrevivientes del clúster (implicando una breve interrupción y un reinicio completo del SO/aplicación), mientras que FT mantiene una copia secundaria en vivo, sincronizada continuamente en lockstep en otro host, permitiendo una toma de control instantánea sin reinicio ni pérdida de estado en memoria.

questions.name: VMs / FT / DRS
questions.question: Why might an organization choose to protect only a small subset of its most critical VMs with Fault Tolerance (FT) rather than enabling it broadly across every VM in the environment?

options.A: FT can only ever be enabled on a single VM per entire data center, making broad adoption not supported regardless of resource considerations
options.B: Organizations avoid FT because it is fundamentally incompatible with virtualized environments and only works on physical, non-virtualized servers
options.C: FT is typically resource-intensive (requiring a fully synchronized secondary VM consuming equivalent compute resources on another host) and often comes with certain configuration limitations, so it is usually reserved for the small number of truly mission-critical workloads that justify that overhead, while less critical VMs rely on more resource-efficient protection like HA
options.D: FT has little resource cost and is always the default recommended protection method for every single VM without exception

questions.explanation_es: FT suele ser intensivo en recursos (requiere una VM secundaria completamente sincronizada, consumiendo recursos de cómputo equivalentes en otro host) y suele venir con ciertas limitaciones de configuración, por lo que suele reservarse para el pequeño número de cargas verdaderamente críticas que justifican ese costo, mientras que las VMs menos críticas dependen de una protección más eficiente en recursos como HA.

questions.name: VMs / FT / DRS
questions.question: What is a 'VM snapshot', and how does it differ from a full backup of a virtual machine?

options.A: A snapshot captures the VM's disk/memory state at a point in time (often used for short-term rollback during changes like a software upgrade) and is typically stored on the same underlying storage/host as the VM itself, whereas a full backup is generally an independent copy stored separately, intended for longer-term recovery even if the original VM and its storage are lost entirely
options.B: A snapshot permanently deletes the VM's original disk once taken, requiring the snapshot itself to boot the VM from that point forward
options.C: Full backups can only be taken while a VM is powered off, and snapshots can only be taken while a VM is completely deleted
options.D: A snapshot creates a full, storage-independent copy of the VM's disk files on separate physical media at the moment it is taken, providing the same protection against loss of the original datastore that a dedicated backup product would provide, making regularly scheduled snapshots a viable substitute for full backups in most environments

questions.explanation_es: Un snapshot captura el estado de disco/memoria de la VM en un momento dado (a menudo usado para poder revertir a corto plazo durante cambios como una actualización de software) y típicamente se almacena en el mismo storage/host subyacente que la VM, mientras que un backup completo suele ser una copia independiente almacenada por separado, pensada para recuperación a más largo plazo incluso si se pierde la VM original y su storage por completo.

questions.name: VMs / FT / DRS
questions.question: How does 'VM encapsulation' (the fact that a VM is essentially a set of files) benefit disaster recovery (DR) strategies?

options.A: Because a VM's entire state is represented as portable files, those files can be replicated to a secondary site's storage, and the VM can be powered on at that secondary site relatively quickly during a disaster, without needing to physically ship or rebuild hardware, unlike recovering a traditional physical server
options.B: VM encapsulation has little relevance to disaster recovery and only matters for day-to-day operational tasks
options.C: VM encapsulation requires physically transporting the host server's hard drive to the DR site by courier before any recovery can occur, since a VM's files are assumed to be permanently bound to the specific physical disk controller they were created on and unreadable by any storage hardware at another site, even when that site uses an identical make and model of array
options.D: Encapsulated VMs cannot be replicated to any other site making them worse for DR than physical servers

questions.explanation_es: Como el estado completo de una VM se representa como archivos portables, esos archivos pueden replicarse hacia el storage de un sitio secundario, y la VM puede encenderse en ese sitio secundario relativamente rápido durante un desastre, sin necesitar enviar físicamente o reconstruir hardware — a diferencia de recuperar un servidor físico tradicional.

questions.name: VMs / FT / DRS
questions.question: What is the general purpose of a 'resource pool' in a virtualization cluster managed with DRS?

options.A: A resource pool refers to a physical rack of unused, uninstalled servers sitting in storage, unrelated to any active virtualization configuration
options.B: A resource pool logically groups a set of CPU/memory resources and can have limits, reservations, and shares configured on it, allowing an administrator to allocate and prioritize resources among different groups of VMs (e.g., production vs. test/dev) without managing each individual VM's resource settings one by one
options.C: Resource pools can only be created for storage capacity and have no relationship to CPU or memory allocation
options.D: A resource pool automatically deletes any VM that has not been powered on within the last 24 hours

questions.explanation_es: Un resource pool agrupa lógicamente un conjunto de recursos de CPU/memoria y puede tener límites, reservas y shares configurados, permitiendo que un administrador asigne y priorice recursos entre distintos grupos de VMs (por ejemplo, producción vs. test/dev) sin tener que gestionar la configuración de recursos de cada VM individualmente.

questions.name: vSwitch/OVS
questions.question: What is the purpose of NIC teaming (uplink bonding) configured on a vSwitch's set of physical uplinks?

options.A: NIC teaming disables all but one physical NIC permanently, with the others serving no functional purpose at all
options.B: NIC teaming combines multiple physical NICs into a logical uplink group on the vSwitch, providing redundancy (if one physical NIC/link fails, traffic continues over the others) and/or load distribution of outbound traffic across the available physical uplinks
options.C: NIC teaming works by assigning a separate IP address to each physical uplink and relying on DNS round-robin between them, rather than presenting the bundled physical NICs as a single logical uplink to the vSwitch
options.D: NIC teaming requires every VM on the host to share a single virtual NIC, regardless of how many physical uplinks exist

questions.explanation_es: El NIC teaming combina varias NICs físicas en un grupo de uplink lógico en el vSwitch, dando redundancia (si falla una NIC/enlace físico, el tráfico continúa por las demás) y/o distribución de carga del tráfico saliente entre los uplinks físicos disponibles.

questions.name: vSwitch/OVS
questions.question: What does 'promiscuous mode' mean when configured on a vSwitch port group, and why is it typically disabled by default?

options.A: Promiscuous mode has little security implications and is disabled by default only because it slightly increases the vSwitch's power consumption, since the additional CPU cycles spent copying every frame to every virtual NIC on the port group were found in early benchmarks to measurably raise host power draw under sustained heavy traffic loads
options.B: Promiscuous mode automatically encrypts all traffic on the port group and is disabled by default purely to save CPU resources
options.C: Promiscuous mode allows a VM's virtual NIC to see all traffic passing through the port group's virtual switch, not just traffic addressed to its own MAC address; it's disabled by default because it would otherwise let one VM potentially observe traffic intended for other VMs sharing that port group, which is a security concern
options.D: Promiscuous mode only affects physical switches and has no meaningful equivalent setting on any vSwitch

questions.explanation_es: El modo promiscuo permite que la NIC virtual de una VM vea todo el tráfico que pasa por el switch virtual de ese port group, no solo el tráfico dirigido a su propia MAC; está deshabilitado por defecto porque de lo contrario una VM podría observar tráfico destinado a otras VMs del mismo port group, lo cual es una preocupación de seguridad.

questions.name: vSwitch/OVS
questions.question: In Open vSwitch (OVS), what is a 'bridge', and how does it relate to physical and virtual interfaces on the host?

options.A: OVS bridges have no relationship to virtual machine networking and are used only for physical cable management labeling
options.B: An OVS bridge can only ever have exactly one single port attached to it, making it functionally identical to a single Ethernet cable, a limitation carried over from the original Linux bridge kernel module that early OVS releases were built on top of before adding true multi-port switching
options.C: An OVS bridge is a logical switch instance to which virtual machine interfaces (vNICs) and physical NICs can be attached as ports, allowing OVS to switch traffic between them, similar in concept to a VLAN-aware virtual switch instance
options.D: An OVS bridge refers to a physical cable connecting two separate data centers together

questions.explanation_es: Un bridge de OVS es una instancia de switch lógico a la que se pueden conectar interfaces de máquinas virtuales (vNICs) y NICs físicas como puertos, permitiendo que OVS conmute tráfico entre ellas — conceptualmente similar a una instancia de switch virtual con soporte de VLAN.

questions.name: vSwitch/OVS
questions.question: How does OVS's support for the OpenFlow protocol change how forwarding decisions can be made, compared to a purely traditional MAC-learning switch?

options.A: OpenFlow disables all MAC learning capability permanently and forces every OVS instance to operate purely as a Layer 1 repeater
options.B: OpenFlow's controller channel is used mainly to collect port statistics and interface counters from OVS for monitoring purposes, while the actual flow-matching and forwarding-table entries continue to be populated through OVS's own local MAC-learning process rather than being installed by the controller
options.C: OpenFlow allows an external SDN controller to programmatically install fine-grained flow-matching rules directly into OVS's forwarding tables (matching on fields well beyond just destination MAC, such as IP, port, or other header fields), enabling centralized, software-defined control over forwarding behavior rather than relying solely on autonomous local MAC learning
options.D: OpenFlow has no effect on forwarding behavior at all and is used for firmware update delivery to the switch

questions.explanation_es: OpenFlow permite que un controlador SDN externo instale programáticamente reglas de coincidencia de flujo detalladas directamente en las tablas de reenvío de OVS (haciendo match en campos mucho más allá de la MAC destino, como IP, puerto, u otros campos del encabezado), habilitando control centralizado y definido por software sobre el comportamiento de reenvío, en lugar de depender únicamente del aprendizaje autónomo de MAC local.

questions.name: vSwitch/OVS
questions.question: Why is a vSwitch/OVS instance generally considered a critical point to secure and monitor within a virtualized or NFV (Network Functions Virtualization) environment?

options.A: vSwitches are only relevant to storage networking and play no role in general data-plane traffic security
options.B: Because the vSwitch handles all traffic between co-located VMs and out to the physical network on that host, a misconfiguration or compromise at the vSwitch level (e.g., incorrect VLAN/port group assignment, or a compromised OVS controller in an SDN deployment) could expose sensitive intra-host traffic or allow traffic to cross security boundaries it should not
options.C: The vSwitch has little security relevance, since it operates entirely below the layer where any meaningful traffic manipulation, filtering, or misconfiguration could ever occur
options.D: Securing a vSwitch is only necessary in a Type 2 hypervisor environment and never in a Type 1 (bare-metal) enterprise deployment

questions.explanation_es: Como el vSwitch maneja todo el tráfico entre VMs coubicadas y hacia la red física desde ese host, una mala configuración o un compromiso a nivel de vSwitch (por ejemplo, una asignación incorrecta de VLAN/port group, o un controlador OVS comprometido en un despliegue SDN) podría exponer tráfico sensible entre VMs o permitir que el tráfico cruce límites de seguridad que no debería cruzar.

questions.name: VRF
questions.question: How does a router with multiple VRFs configured decide which routing table to use when making a forwarding decision for a given incoming packet?

options.A: The router uses the routing table (RIB) associated with the VRF that the packet's ingress interface belongs to, since each VRF maintains its own separate, independent routing table used only for traffic entering (or destined to leave) via interfaces assigned to that same VRF
options.B: The router selects which routing table to use based on the packet's source IP subnet rather than the ingress interface's VRF assignment, so two interfaces placed in different VRFs but sharing the same IP subnet range would still resolve to a single shared lookup table
options.C: VRF routing table selection depends solely on the packet's destination MAC address, with no relevance to the ingress interface's VRF assignment
options.D: The router randomly selects one of the configured VRF routing tables for each packet, with no deterministic relationship to the ingress interface

questions.explanation_es: El router usa la tabla de enrutamiento (RIB) asociada a la VRF a la que pertenece la interfaz de ingreso del paquete, ya que cada VRF mantiene su propia tabla de enrutamiento separada e independiente, usada solo para tráfico que entra (o debe salir) por interfaces asignadas a esa misma VRF.

questions.name: VRF
questions.question: What is the role of Multiprotocol BGP (MP-BGP) with route-distinguishers (RD) and route-targets (RT) in a full MPLS L3VPN deployment using VRFs, as opposed to simple VRF-lite?

options.A: MP-BGP with RD/RT is used to negotiate MTU and tunnel encapsulation parameters between PE routers, rather than to distinguish overlapping customer prefixes or to control which VRFs import and export specific routes
options.B: MP-BGP is required even for a single-router VRF-lite deployment with no MPLS core involved at all
options.C: Route-distinguishers and route-targets serve no functional purpose and exist purely for historical/legacy documentation reasons, left over from early IETF drafts of RFC 2547 that used a different mechanism to differentiate customer routes, retained in modern implementations purely for backward compatibility with legacy PE line cards from that era, none of which remain in production on any current large-scale provider network today
options.D: MP-BGP with RD/RT allows a provider's core network to carry potentially overlapping customer VPN prefixes across multiple PE routers by making each VPN prefix unique (via the RD) and controlling which VRFs import/export which routes (via RT), enabling VRF routes to be distributed dynamically across the MPLS core rather than relying on manually configured point-to-point sub-interfaces per VRF like VRF-lite typically does

questions.explanation_es: MP-BGP con RD/RT permite que el core de un proveedor transporte prefijos VPN de clientes potencialmente superpuestos a través de múltiples routers PE, haciendo único cada prefijo VPN (vía el RD) y controlando qué VRFs importan/exportan qué rutas (vía RT), permitiendo distribuir dinámicamente las rutas de VRF a través del core MPLS, en lugar de depender de sub-interfaces punto a punto configuradas manualmente por VRF como suele hacer VRF-lite.

questions.name: VRF
questions.question: Why might a service provider use VRFs to offer 'MPLS L3VPN' services to multiple separate customers over a shared physical network infrastructure?

options.A: VRFs are used purely for internal network management labeling and have no effect on actual customer traffic isolation
options.B: A provider can only support a single customer VRF per physical router chassis, limiting VRF-based multi-tenancy to very small deployments
options.C: VRFs require the provider to build a completely separate physical fiber network for each individual customer, providing no actual infrastructure sharing benefit at all, because each VRF's forwarding table must be tied to its own dedicated set of physical interface cards on the PE router rather than being able to share common uplinks
options.D: VRFs allow the provider to keep each customer's routes and traffic logically isolated from every other customer sharing the same physical PE routers and core links, even though multiple customers' traffic physically traverses the same shared infrastructure, without requiring a dedicated physical network per customer

questions.explanation_es: Las VRFs permiten al proveedor mantener las rutas y el tráfico de cada cliente lógicamente aislados de los demás clientes que comparten los mismos routers PE y enlaces de core físicos, aunque el tráfico de varios clientes atraviese físicamente la misma infraestructura compartida, sin necesitar una red física dedicada por cliente — la base del servicio MPLS L3VPN.

questions.name: VRF
questions.question: What command is commonly used on a Cisco IOS/IOS-XE router to view the routing table specific to a particular VRF, rather than the global routing table?

options.A: VRF-specific routing tables can never be viewed independently; only the combined global table is ever displayed by any IOS command, a limitation only partially addressed later by 'show vrf'
options.B: 'show vlan brief' is the only command capable of displaying VRF-specific routing information
options.C: 'show ip route vrf <name>' displays the routing table specific to the named VRF, as distinct from 'show ip route' which displays the global routing table
options.D: 'show interfaces status' displays per-VRF routing table contents alongside interface link status

questions.explanation_es: 'show ip route vrf <nombre>' muestra la tabla de enrutamiento específica de la VRF indicada, a diferencia de 'show ip route' que muestra la tabla de enrutamiento global — un comando básico para verificar el contenido de una VRF en particular durante troubleshooting.

questions.name: VRF
questions.question: In a campus network segmentation design, what is a practical reason to place guest wireless traffic into its own dedicated VRF, separate from the corporate/employee VRF?

options.A: Using a separate VRF for guest traffic guarantees that guest devices will automatically receive faster internet bandwidth than corporate devices
options.B: Placing guest traffic in a separate VRF ensures that guest devices, by default, cannot route to corporate resources via that VRF's routing table, providing a strong baseline of network-layer isolation between guest and corporate traffic without relying solely on VLAN/ACL-based separation
options.C: VRFs have no relevance to guest network isolation and are used for voice traffic prioritization
options.D: VRF-based guest isolation requires physically separate cabling from every guest access point back to the core, with no shared infrastructure possible, since VRF forwarding tables are tied to specific physical ports at the hardware ASIC level and cannot be associated with traffic arriving over a shared trunk or SVI

questions.explanation_es: Colocar el tráfico de invitados en su propia VRF asegura que, por defecto, los dispositivos de invitados no puedan enrutar hacia recursos corporativos a través de la tabla de enrutamiento de esa VRF, dando una base sólida de aislamiento a nivel de red entre tráfico de invitados y corporativo, sin depender únicamente de separación por VLAN/ACL.

questions.name: VRF
questions.question: What happens to a router's global routing table entries (e.g., directly connected or statically configured routes on non-VRF interfaces) once some interfaces are moved into custom VRFs, while others remain outside any VRF?

options.A: Moving any interface into a VRF immediately deletes every route in the router's global routing table, including routes unrelated to the VRF-assigned interfaces
options.B: A router can only ever have either VRFs configured or a global routing table, never both simultaneously
options.C: Interfaces that remain unassigned to any custom VRF continue to use the router's default/global routing table, operating exactly as they did before any VRF was configured, while only the interfaces explicitly assigned to a custom VRF use that VRF's separate routing table
options.D: All interfaces on the router, whether assigned to a VRF or not, are automatically forced to share a single combined routing table the moment any VRF is configured anywhere on the device, since the router's control plane is described as maintaining only one active RIB process regardless of how many VRFs exist

questions.explanation_es: Las interfaces que permanecen sin asignar a ninguna VRF personalizada siguen usando la tabla de enrutamiento default/global del router, operando exactamente igual que antes de configurar cualquier VRF, mientras que solo las interfaces explícitamente asignadas a una VRF personalizada usan la tabla separada de esa VRF.

questions.name: VRF
questions.question: Why is it important to verify which VRF a troubleshooting command (like ping or traceroute) is actually operating in, when a router has multiple VRFs configured?

options.A: Ping and traceroute automatically use whichever VRF the destination address happens to belong to, determined by checking every configured VRF table in sequence until a match is found, so specifying a VRF explicitly only matters when the address exists in more than one VRF at once
options.B: By default, commands like ping/traceroute typically operate against the global routing table unless explicitly told to use a specific VRF (e.g., 'ping vrf <name> <address>'), so failing to specify the correct VRF could lead to a misleading result — for example, a failed ping against the wrong table when the destination is actually reachable within a different VRF
options.C: VRF has little bearing on how ping or traceroute operate; these commands always ignore VRF configuration entirely
options.D: Specifying the wrong VRF in a ping command will always cause the router itself to crash and reboot

questions.explanation_es: Por defecto, comandos como ping/traceroute suelen operar contra la tabla de enrutamiento global a menos que se les indique explícitamente usar una VRF específica (por ejemplo, 'ping vrf <nombre> <dirección>'), así que no especificar la VRF correcta podría llevar a un resultado engañoso — por ejemplo, un ping fallido contra la tabla equivocada cuando el destino en realidad es alcanzable dentro de otra VRF.

questions.name: VRF
questions.question: How does the concept of a VRF relate to the broader idea of 'network virtualization' at Layer 3?

options.A: A VRF creates a separate Layer 2 broadcast domain analogous to a VLAN, but all VRFs configured on a device continue to share the same single Layer 3 routing table when making forwarding decisions
options.B: VRF is unrelated to network virtualization and refers to a physical hardware add-on card that must be purchased separately
options.C: A VRF is a form of Layer 3 network virtualization: it creates a logically separate, independent instance of the routing/forwarding function on a single physical device, similar in spirit to how a hypervisor creates logically separate VMs on a single physical server
options.D: Network virtualization and VRF are mutually exclusive concepts, and a device supporting VRFs cannot be considered virtualized in any sense, since true network virtualization was defined by early SDN literature to require decoupling the control plane onto a separate physical controller, which VRF alone does not do

questions.explanation_es: Una VRF es una forma de virtualización de red en Capa 3: crea una instancia lógicamente separada e independiente de la función de enrutamiento/reenvío en un único dispositivo físico, de forma conceptualmente similar a cómo un hypervisor crea VMs lógicamente separadas en un único servidor físico.

questions.name: GRE / IPsec / AH
questions.question: What does the GRE header primarily contain, and what is its main function within an encapsulated packet?

options.A: The GRE header contains the full encryption key material needed to decrypt the payload at the remote end, making GRE inherently as secure as IPsec, since the protocol-type field in the GRE header is sometimes mistaken for a key field because it occupies a similarly-sized portion of the header immediately after the flags
options.B: The GRE header is functionally identical to a standard Ethernet header and operates only at Layer 2
options.C: The GRE header carries routing protocol hello packets and cannot encapsulate any other type of payload
options.D: The GRE header identifies the protocol type of the payload being encapsulated (allowing GRE to carry many different protocol types inside an IP packet) and provides basic encapsulation framing, without itself providing encryption, authentication, or reliable delivery

questions.explanation_es: El encabezado GRE principalmente identifica el tipo de protocolo del payload encapsulado (permitiendo que GRE transporte muchos tipos de protocolo distintos dentro de un paquete IP) y provee el framing básico de encapsulación, sin proveer por sí mismo cifrado, autenticación, ni entrega confiable.

questions.name: GRE / IPsec / AH
questions.question: In IPsec, what is the role of IKE (Internet Key Exchange) relative to AH and ESP?

options.A: IKE is responsible for encrypting user data packets directly, while AH and ESP are used only to negotiate encryption keys
options.B: IKE is the protocol used to negotiate and establish the Security Associations (SAs) — including the shared cryptographic keys and security parameters — that AH and/or ESP then use to actually authenticate/encrypt traffic; AH and ESP handle the data-plane protection, while IKE handles the control-plane key negotiation
options.C: IKE is responsible for encrypting and authenticating the user data packets directly once a tunnel is established, while AH and ESP are used only during the initial negotiation phase to agree on which encryption algorithm IKE itself will use
options.D: IKE, AH, and ESP are three interchangeable names for exactly the same single protocol, with no functional distinction between them, a naming convention that emerged because all three were originally bundled into a single RFC before later revisions split key-negotiation from data-plane protection without changing the underlying protocol behavior

questions.explanation_es: IKE (Internet Key Exchange) es el protocolo usado para negociar y establecer las Asociaciones de Seguridad (SA) — incluyendo las claves criptográficas compartidas y los parámetros de seguridad — que luego AH y/o ESP usan para realmente autenticar/cifrar el tráfico; AH y ESP manejan la protección del plano de datos, mientras IKE maneja la negociación de claves del plano de control.

questions.name: GRE / IPsec / AH
questions.question: Why does AH (Authentication Header) have compatibility problems with NAT (Network Address Translation) that ESP generally does not have to the same degree?

options.A: AH cannot be used over any IP network at all, regardless of whether NAT is present, making the NAT compatibility question irrelevant, a restriction dating back to AH's original design assumption that IP addresses would never be rewritten anywhere along the path, which is why later IPsec implementations effectively deprecated AH in favor of ESP for nearly all deployments rather than attempting to patch AH's header-integrity check to tolerate any address translation
options.B: ESP's authentication in transport mode covers the entire outer IP header, including the source and destination addresses, making it just as sensitive to NAT's address rewriting as AH is, which is why NAT-T is required equally for both protocols
options.C: AH's integrity check includes portions of the outer IP header itself (including source/destination IP addresses) in its cryptographic hash, so if NAT modifies those IP addresses in transit, the AH integrity check fails at the receiver; ESP's authentication (in transport mode) does not cover the outer IP header in the same way, making it more NAT-tolerant, particularly when combined with NAT-Traversal (NAT-T) techniques for tunnel mode
options.D: AH remains fully compatible with NAT because its integrity check is computed only over the ESP header and payload, excluding the outer IP addresses entirely, which is the same scope of coverage ESP uses in transport mode

questions.explanation_es: La verificación de integridad de AH incluye porciones del propio encabezado IP externo (incluyendo las direcciones IP origen/destino) en su hash criptográfico, así que si NAT modifica esas direcciones IP en tránsito, la verificación de integridad de AH falla en el receptor; la autenticación de ESP (en modo transporte) no cubre el encabezado IP externo de la misma forma, haciéndolo más tolerante a NAT, especialmente combinado con técnicas de NAT-Traversal (NAT-T) en modo túnel.

questions.name: GRE / IPsec / AH
questions.question: What is a Security Association (SA) in the context of IPsec?

options.A: An SA is a bidirectional relationship requiring only a single instance total, regardless of how many directions of traffic need protection
options.B: An SA refers to a single, globally shared encryption key used identically by every IPsec deployment worldwide, with no per-session negotiation involved, a design meant to simplify vendor interoperability by shipping every IPsec device preconfigured with the same factory-default key material, so no separate negotiation step would ever be required
options.C: An SA is a physical cable connector standard used for fiber-optic IPsec links
options.D: An SA is a unidirectional logical relationship between two IPsec peers that defines the security parameters (encryption algorithm, authentication method, keys, and lifetime) used to protect traffic in one direction, meaning a typical bidirectional IPsec session requires at least two SAs (one for each direction)

questions.explanation_es: Una SA (Security Association) es una relación lógica unidireccional entre dos peers IPsec que define los parámetros de seguridad (algoritmo de cifrado, método de autenticación, claves y tiempo de vida) usados para proteger el tráfico en una dirección, lo que significa que una sesión IPsec bidireccional típica requiere al menos dos SAs (una por cada dirección).

questions.name: GRE / IPsec / AH
questions.question: Why is 'GRE over IPsec' (or IPsec protecting a GRE tunnel) a common design pattern instead of using plain IPsec tunnel mode alone for a site-to-site VPN that must carry a dynamic routing protocol?

options.A: GRE over IPsec is used purely for historical compatibility with 1990s hardware and offers no functional advantage on any modern platform
options.B: Plain IPsec tunnel mode natively supports multicast traffic by replicating each multicast packet as a separate unicast copy per peer at the IKEv2 layer, so GRE over IPsec is mainly used instead to reduce encryption overhead rather than to enable multicast or routing-protocol support
options.C: GRE over IPsec is required only when the VPN needs to carry HTTP traffic and serves no other purpose
options.D: Plain IPsec tunnel mode alone generally does not support carrying multicast traffic (which dynamic routing protocols like OSPF or EIGRP rely on for neighbor discovery), whereas GRE can encapsulate that multicast/routing-protocol traffic into a regular unicast IP packet first, which IPsec can then protect end-to-end, combining GRE's protocol flexibility with IPsec's confidentiality/integrity

questions.explanation_es: IPsec en modo túnel puro generalmente no soporta transportar tráfico multicast (del cual dependen protocolos de enrutamiento dinámico como OSPF o EIGRP para el descubrimiento de vecinos), mientras que GRE puede encapsular ese tráfico multicast/de protocolo de enrutamiento en un paquete IP unicast normal primero, que IPsec puede luego proteger de extremo a extremo, combinando la flexibilidad de protocolo de GRE con la confidencialidad/integridad de IPsec.

questions.name: GRE / IPsec / AH
questions.question: What does 'Perfect Forward Secrecy' (PFS) provide when enabled as part of an IPsec IKE negotiation?

options.A: PFS eliminates the need for any encryption key at all, allowing IPsec to operate with zero cryptographic overhead, because the Diffie-Hellman exchange PFS relies on is assumed to generate a permanent shared secret during the very first negotiation that all subsequent sessions can simply reuse without performing any further key derivation or encryption computation
options.B: PFS guarantees that IPsec traffic will never experience any packet loss under any network condition
options.C: PFS ensures that even if a long-term key (or a past session key) is later compromised, previously captured/recorded encrypted traffic from earlier sessions cannot be decrypted, because each session's actual encryption keys are derived using fresh, independent key exchange material rather than being simply derived from a single long-term shared secret
options.D: PFS refers to a physical security camera feature unrelated to any cryptographic property of IPsec

questions.explanation_es: PFS (Perfect Forward Secrecy) asegura que, aunque una clave de largo plazo (o una clave de sesión pasada) se vea comprometida más adelante, el tráfico cifrado capturado/registrado previamente de sesiones anteriores no pueda descifrarse, porque las claves de cifrado reales de cada sesión se derivan usando material de intercambio de claves fresco e independiente, en lugar de derivarse simplemente de un único secreto compartido de largo plazo.

questions.name: GRE / IPsec / AH
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes IPsec's 'transport mode' as opposed to 'tunnel mode'?

options.A: Tunnel mode can only be used for host-to-host traffic and can never be used for site-to-site gateway-to-gateway VPNs
options.B: Transport mode and tunnel mode are functionally identical, and the terms are used interchangeably with no configuration difference between them
options.C: In transport mode, the original IP header is preserved and only the payload (and, depending on AH/ESP, part of the header) is protected, making transport mode typically used for host-to-host communication rather than for encapsulating traffic between two gateways representing entire networks behind them, which is what tunnel mode is commonly used for
options.D: Transport mode always adds a completely new outer IP header, exactly like tunnel mode, with the two modes differing only in encryption algorithm choice, a distinction some administrators mistakenly rely on when selecting AES over 3DES, assuming the choice of cipher rather than the header structure is what determines whether the mode is suitable for gateway-to-gateway deployments

questions.explanation_es: En modo transporte, se preserva el encabezado IP original y solo se protege el payload (y, según AH/ESP, parte del encabezado), por lo que el modo transporte suele usarse para comunicación host-a-host en vez de para encapsular tráfico entre dos gateways que representan redes enteras detrás de ellos, que es para lo que se usa comúnmente el modo túnel.

questions.name: GRE / IPsec / AH
questions.question: What is a key operational difference to consider when troubleshooting a GRE tunnel that is reported as 'up/up' at the interface level but is not actually passing traffic correctly?

options.A: A GRE tunnel interface can never show as 'up/up' unless every single type of traffic that could ever traverse it is already flowing correctly with zero packet loss
options.B: A GRE tunnel interface can show as administratively and line-protocol 'up' based purely on reachability to the tunnel destination IP, even if there is a problem further along the path (such as an ACL blocking GRE protocol 47, an MTU/fragmentation issue, or a routing problem for traffic meant to traverse the tunnel), so 'up/up' status alone does not guarantee the tunnel is fully functional end-to-end for actual data traffic
options.C: GRE tunnels have no concept of interface state at all and never display any up/down status in 'show interface' output
options.D: An 'up/up' GRE tunnel interface guarantees that IPsec encryption (if configured) is also fully operational with no possibility of a separate IPsec-layer failure

questions.explanation_es: Una interfaz de túnel GRE puede mostrarse como 'up/up' basándose únicamente en la alcanzabilidad hacia la IP destino del túnel, aunque exista un problema más adelante en el camino (como una ACL bloqueando el protocolo GRE 47, un problema de MTU/fragmentación, o un problema de enrutamiento para el tráfico que debería atravesar el túnel), así que el estado 'up/up' por sí solo no garantiza que el túnel esté completamente funcional de extremo a extremo para el tráfico de datos real.

questions.name: GRE / IPsec / AH
questions.question: Why might MTU and fragmentation be a particular concern when using GRE and/or IPsec tunnels compared to native, unencapsulated IP traffic?

options.A: Each layer of encapsulation (GRE header, and additionally IPsec/ESP header and trailer) adds extra bytes of overhead to the original packet, which can push the total packet size above the path's MTU, causing fragmentation (or, if the Don't Fragment bit is set and fragmentation isn't allowed, causing the packet to be dropped) unless the tunnel interface's MTU is adjusted or path MTU discovery is properly handled
options.B: MTU has no relevance to tunneled traffic, since tunnel interfaces are exempt from all IP fragmentation rules by design
options.C: GRE and IPsec encapsulation always reduce the total packet size, so MTU and fragmentation concerns only apply to unencapsulated native IP traffic, never to tunneled traffic, because both protocols are assumed to compress the original payload's header fields as part of encapsulation, a behavior sometimes confused with actual header compression features found in unrelated protocols like RTP or TCP header compression over slow links
options.D: Fragmentation concerns apply only to IPv6 tunnels and have no relevance to IPv4-based GRE or IPsec tunnels

questions.explanation_es: Cada capa de encapsulación (encabezado GRE, y adicionalmente encabezado y trailer de IPsec/ESP) agrega bytes extra de overhead al paquete original, lo cual puede empujar el tamaño total del paquete por encima del MTU del camino, causando fragmentación (o, si el bit Don't Fragment está activo y no se permite fragmentar, causando que el paquete se descarte) a menos que se ajuste el MTU de la interfaz de túnel o se maneje correctamente el descubrimiento de MTU de camino.

questions.name: LISP
questions.question: What is the function of the ITR (Ingress Tunnel Router) in a LISP deployment?

options.A: The ITR receives packets from a local EID-addressed source destined for a remote EID, queries the mapping system (via a Map-Resolver) to learn the destination's current RLOC if not already cached, and then encapsulates the original packet in a LISP header to be delivered to that RLOC
options.B: The ITR only receives already-encapsulated LISP traffic from remote sites and decapsulates it; it never originates encapsulation itself
options.C: The ITR is responsible for assigning DHCP leases to endpoints inside the LISP site and has no role in encapsulation
options.D: The ITR replaces the need for any Map-Server in the LISP architecture, performing that role itself

questions.explanation_es: El ITR (Ingress Tunnel Router) recibe paquetes de una fuente local direccionada por EID destinados a un EID remoto, consulta el sistema de mapeo (vía un Map-Resolver) para aprender el RLOC actual del destino si aún no está en caché, y luego encapsula el paquete original en un encabezado LISP para entregarlo a ese RLOC.

questions.name: LISP
questions.question: Why does LISP maintain a local 'map-cache' on ITRs, and what happens when that cache does not have an entry for a given destination EID?

options.A: The map-cache is purely optional and provides no performance benefit, since every single packet always triggers a fresh map-request regardless of prior lookups, a behavior intentionally chosen so that the mapping system always has the most current RLOC information rather than risking forwarding traffic based on an entry that may have become stale since it was first learned
options.B: A map-cache miss causes the ITR to permanently block all future traffic to that destination EID until the device is manually rebooted
options.C: The map-cache stores only the RLOC addresses belonging to the local site's own ETRs, and is consulted solely to pick which local egress interface to use, rather than caching EID-to-RLOC mappings learned for remote destinations
options.D: The map-cache stores recently learned EID-to-RLOC mappings so subsequent packets to the same destination can be encapsulated immediately without a new lookup; if there is no cached entry (a 'cache miss'), the ITR sends a map-request to the mapping system (Map-Resolver/Map-Server) to learn the correct RLOC before it can encapsulate and forward the packet

questions.explanation_es: El map-cache almacena mapeos EID-a-RLOC aprendidos recientemente para que los paquetes subsiguientes hacia el mismo destino puedan encapsularse de inmediato sin una nueva consulta; si no hay una entrada en caché (un 'cache miss'), el ITR envía un map-request al sistema de mapeo (Map-Resolver/Map-Server) para aprender el RLOC correcto antes de poder encapsular y reenviar el paquete.

questions.name: LISP
questions.question: How does LISP support endpoint mobility (e.g., a host moving between sites) without requiring the endpoint to change its own IP address?

options.A: LISP requires every mobile endpoint to obtain a completely new IP address every single time it physically moves to a different location
options.B: LISP has no mechanism to support endpoint mobility and endpoints must remain permanently in a single fixed location
options.C: LISP mobility support requires the endpoint itself to run a dedicated LISP software client that manually re-registers its own IP address with a central DNS server
options.D: Because LISP separates identity (EID) from location (RLOC), when a host moves to a new site, only the RLOC associated with its EID needs to be updated in the mapping system (by the new site's xTR registering the host); the host's own EID address never has to change, and traffic destined to it is simply re-encapsulated toward the new RLOC once the mapping updates propagate

questions.explanation_es: Como LISP separa identidad (EID) de ubicación (RLOC), cuando un host se mueve a un sitio nuevo, solo hace falta actualizar en el sistema de mapeo el RLOC asociado a su EID (registrado por el xTR del nuevo sitio); la dirección EID del host nunca tiene que cambiar, y el tráfico dirigido a él simplemente se vuelve a encapsular hacia el nuevo RLOC una vez que se propaga la actualización del mapeo.

questions.name: LISP
questions.question: What is the general structure of a LISP-encapsulated data packet (LISP data encapsulation)?

options.A: LISP-encapsulated packets carry no outer IP header at all and are transported purely at Layer 2 using MAC addressing only
options.B: LISP encapsulation completely discards the original packet's addressing information and replaces it entirely with a brand new packet containing no relationship to the original data, generating a fresh EID pair at the ETR based purely on the destination RLOC, which is why LISP is described as requiring re-addressing at every hop
options.C: LISP encapsulation uses TCP as its outer transport protocol, never UDP
options.D: The original packet (with its EID source/destination addressing intact) is encapsulated inside a UDP/IP packet, where the outer IP header uses RLOC addresses for actual routing across the underlying transport network, with a LISP header between the outer UDP header and the original inner packet

questions.explanation_es: El paquete original (con su direccionamiento EID origen/destino intacto) se encapsula dentro de un paquete UDP/IP, donde el encabezado IP externo usa direcciones RLOC para el enrutamiento real a través de la red de transporte subyacente, con un encabezado LISP entre el encabezado UDP externo y el paquete interno original.

questions.name: LISP
questions.question: What role does an ETR (Egress Tunnel Router) play once it receives a LISP-encapsulated packet destined for one of its locally registered EIDs?

options.A: An ETR can only ever process packets originally sent using plain unencapsulated IP, and cannot decapsulate any LISP header at all
options.B: The ETR re-encapsulates the packet a second time with an entirely new, unrelated destination before forwarding it anywhere
options.C: The ETR decapsulates the LISP header (removing the outer RLOC-addressed transport wrapper) and forwards the original inner packet toward its final local EID destination, delivering the packet as it would have looked before it was ever encapsulated by the remote ITR
options.D: The ETR discards every LISP-encapsulated packet it receives without any further processing, since ETRs are read-only monitoring devices with no forwarding capability, their role being limited to passively logging EID reachability statistics for the mapping system rather than participating in the actual data path

questions.explanation_es: El ETR decapsula el encabezado LISP (quitando la envoltura de transporte externa direccionada por RLOC) y reenvía el paquete interno original hacia su destino EID local final, entregando el paquete tal como se veía antes de que el ITR remoto lo encapsulara.

questions.name: LISP
questions.question: Why is LISP sometimes described as providing a more scalable alternative to putting every endpoint's specific /32 (or /128) host route into the global routing table for mobility scenarios?

options.A: LISP requires every single host route to still be injected into the global routing table in exactly the same way as without LISP, providing no scalability benefit at all, since the mapping system is assumed to function only as a passive logging database that must be mirrored back into the core BGP table for routers to actually forward traffic correctly
options.B: LISP keeps detailed per-host EID-to-RLOC mapping information within its own separate mapping system rather than injecting individual host routes into the underlying routing protocol/table, which avoids bloating the core routing table with a massive number of host-specific entries just to support endpoint mobility
options.C: LISP eliminates the need for any routing table on any device in the network, including the mapping system itself
options.D: LISP scalability has nothing to do with routing table size and is purely a marketing claim with no technical basis

questions.explanation_es: LISP mantiene la información detallada de mapeo EID-a-RLOC por host dentro de su propio sistema de mapeo separado, en lugar de inyectar rutas de host individuales en el protocolo/tabla de enrutamiento subyacente, lo cual evita saturar la tabla de enrutamiento del core con una cantidad masiva de entradas específicas de host solo para soportar movilidad de endpoints.

questions.name: LISP
questions.question: In the context of SD-Access, how is the general LISP architecture (ITR/ETR/Map-Server/Map-Resolver) mapped onto SD-Access's own fabric roles?

options.A: LISP roles apply only to wireless SD-Access deployments and have no relevance to wired fabric roles at all
options.B: In SD-Access, the Fabric Edge Node performs the Map-Server/Map-Resolver role, while the Fabric Control Plane node has little LISP-related function, a design choice made so that the same switches handling wireless client onboarding at the access layer could also resolve EID-to-RLOC mappings locally without needing to query a separate control-plane device for every new host
options.C: SD-Access uses LISP concepts only for wireless client roaming between access points, while wired endpoint reachability within the fabric is handled entirely through traditional VLAN-based Layer 2 flooding rather than any EID-to-RLOC mapping
options.D: The Fabric Control Plane node in SD-Access takes on the Map-Server/Map-Resolver role, while Fabric Edge Nodes and Fabric Border Nodes act in xTR-like roles (encapsulating/decapsulating VXLAN traffic and registering endpoint EID-to-RLOC mappings), applying LISP's identity/location separation concepts within the fabric's own architecture

questions.explanation_es: El Fabric Control Plane node de SD-Access asume el rol de Map-Server/Map-Resolver, mientras que los Fabric Edge Node y Fabric Border Node actúan en roles similares a xTR (encapsulando/decapsulando tráfico VXLAN y registrando mapeos EID-a-RLOC de endpoints), aplicando los conceptos de separación identidad/ubicación de LISP dentro de la arquitectura propia de la fabric.

questions.name: LISP
questions.question: What potential latency impact can occur on the very first packet sent to a previously-unseen destination EID in a LISP deployment, and why?

options.A: The first-packet latency concern applies only to packets smaller than 64 bytes and never to any larger packet size
options.B: LISP guarantees that every single packet, including the very first one to any destination, experiences exactly zero additional latency under all circumstances, because the mapping system is assumed to pre-populate every ITR's map-cache with all EID-to-RLOC mappings in the network at boot time, before any traffic is ever sent, eliminating the need for any map-request to occur during normal operation
options.C: The very first packet to a new destination may experience additional latency because the ITR must first perform a map-request/map-reply exchange with the mapping system to learn the destination's RLOC before it can encapsulate and forward that packet, whereas subsequent packets to the same destination benefit from the now-cached mapping and avoid that extra lookup delay
options.D: First-packet latency in LISP occurs because the ITR must first perform an ARP resolution for the destination EID's MAC address before it can even build the map-request message, adding a Layer 2 resolution delay on top of any mapping-system lookup

questions.explanation_es: El primer paquete hacia un destino nuevo puede experimentar latencia adicional porque el ITR primero debe realizar un intercambio de map-request/map-reply con el sistema de mapeo para aprender el RLOC del destino antes de poder encapsular y reenviar ese paquete, mientras que los paquetes subsiguientes hacia el mismo destino se benefician del mapeo ya en caché y evitan ese retraso extra de consulta.

questions.name: LISP
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes how LISP can support multiple 'instance IDs' within a single mapping system, conceptually similar to how VRFs provide multiple routing tables on a router?

options.A: Instance IDs are appended to the RLOC address rather than to the EID, so two devices assigned to different instance IDs can only share the same EID if their underlying RLOC addresses also happen to differ
options.B: A LISP instance ID allows the same EID address space to be reused independently across multiple isolated LISP 'virtual networks' (similar in spirit to how a VRF allows the same IP address range to be reused across isolated routing tables), enabling multi-tenancy within a single shared LISP mapping infrastructure
options.C: A LISP deployment can support only a single instance ID globally, making any form of multi-tenant EID address reuse not supported
options.D: LISP instance IDs have no relationship to multi-tenancy or address reuse and refer only to a device's hardware serial number

questions.explanation_es: Un instance ID de LISP permite reutilizar el mismo espacio de direcciones EID de forma independiente entre múltiples 'virtual networks' LISP aisladas (de forma conceptualmente similar a cómo una VRF permite reutilizar el mismo rango de IP entre tablas de enrutamiento aisladas), habilitando multi-tenencia dentro de una única infraestructura de mapeo LISP compartida — este es justamente el mecanismo que usa SD-Access para separar sus virtual networks.

questions.name: VXLAN EVPN/BUM
questions.question: What is the purpose of EVPN Type-1 (Ethernet Auto-Discovery) routes in a VXLAN EVPN fabric using multihoming?

options.A: Type-1 routes are used to advertise Ethernet Segment auto-discovery information, which supports multihoming scenarios (a device dual-connected to two VTEPs) by enabling fast convergence and split-horizon/aliasing behavior across the redundant links
options.B: Type-1 routes are used to advertise individual host MAC addresses, identical in function to Type-2 routes
options.C: Type-1 routes carry only multicast group membership information and have no relationship to multihoming or Ethernet Segments
options.D: Type-1 routes are used to advertise the individual IP addresses of hosts learned locally on an Ethernet Segment, serving essentially the same function as Type-2 routes but scoped only to multihomed segments rather than to all endpoints

questions.explanation_es: Las rutas Type-1 se usan para anunciar información de auto-descubrimiento de Segmento Ethernet, lo cual soporta escenarios de multihoming (un dispositivo doblemente conectado a dos VTEPs) habilitando convergencia rápida y comportamiento de split-horizon/aliasing a través de los enlaces redundantes.

questions.name: VXLAN EVPN/BUM
questions.question: What does EVPN Type-3 (Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag) route advertise, and why is it needed even in a BGP EVPN control-plane deployment?

options.A: Type-3 routes have no relationship to BUM traffic handling and are used solely for BGP session keepalives
options.B: Type-3 routes advertise, per VNI, which VTEPs are interested in receiving BUM (Broadcast, Unknown-unicast, Multicast) traffic for that VNI, allowing other VTEPs to build the correct ingress-replication or multicast distribution list for BUM traffic even though EVPN handles known-unicast MAC learning via the control plane
options.C: Type-3 routes are used to advertise IP prefix reachability for inter-subnet routing, identical to Type-5 routes
options.D: Type-3 routes carry individual host MAC-to-IP bindings, making them functionally identical to Type-2 routes

questions.explanation_es: Las rutas Type-3 anuncian, por VNI, qué VTEPs están interesados en recibir tráfico BUM (Broadcast, Unknown-unicast, Multicast) para esa VNI, permitiendo que otros VTEPs construyan la lista correcta de replicación por ingreso o distribución multicast para el tráfico BUM, incluso cuando EVPN maneja el aprendizaje de MAC conocidas vía el plano de control.

questions.name: VXLAN EVPN/BUM
questions.question: What is 'symmetric IRB' (Integrated Routing and Bridging) in a VXLAN EVPN fabric, and why is it commonly preferred over 'asymmetric IRB'?

options.A: In symmetric IRB, both the ingress and egress VTEP perform a routing lookup (using a shared, consistently-provisioned L3 VNI) when forwarding inter-subnet traffic, which requires every VTEP to only be provisioned with the L2/L3 VNIs of the VLANs actually needed locally, improving scalability compared to asymmetric IRB, where the ingress VTEP must know about every possible destination VNI in the fabric to route directly to it in a single lookup
options.B: Symmetric IRB refers to a physical cabling requirement where every VTEP must be connected with an identical number of cables, unrelated to routing behavior, said to exist so inter-VTEP traffic load balances evenly across uplinks; under this view, VTEPs with fewer physical connections than their peers require reconfiguration before symmetric IRB can be enabled fabric-wide, since the feature is described as tied to cable count rather than to L3 VNI provisioning consistency
options.C: Asymmetric IRB and symmetric IRB are functionally identical, differing only in which vendor coined each term
options.D: Symmetric IRB means that routing is only ever performed by a single centralized VTEP for the entire fabric, with no distributed routing capability

questions.explanation_es: En symmetric IRB, tanto el VTEP de ingreso como el de egreso realizan una búsqueda de enrutamiento (usando una L3 VNI compartida y provisionada de forma consistente) al reenviar tráfico entre subredes, lo cual requiere que cada VTEP solo esté provisionado con las VNIs de Capa 2/3 que realmente necesita localmente, mejorando la escalabilidad comparado con asymmetric IRB, donde el VTEP de ingreso debe conocer cada posible VNI destino de la fabric para enrutar directamente en una sola búsqueda.

questions.name: VXLAN EVPN/BUM
questions.question: How does EVPN's BGP-based control plane help detect and prevent duplicate MAC address issues (MAC 'move' or 'flapping') across a VXLAN fabric compared to pure data-plane flood-and-learn?

options.A: Duplicate MAC detection in EVPN relies on manually configured static MAC address tables at every single VTEP
options.B: EVPN's control plane has no ability to detect duplicate MAC addresses at all; this can only ever be discovered using data-plane flood-and-learn, because BGP Type-2 routes are assumed to carry only MAC reachability information with no sequence-number field, leaving VTEPs no way to tell which advertisement for a given MAC arrived most recently versus which one is stale, a gap that would have to be closed by comparing local port-security timestamps instead
options.C: Because MAC reachability is advertised and tracked via BGP EVPN Type-2 routes (with sequence numbers), the control plane can detect when the same MAC address is being advertised from two different VTEPs nearly simultaneously (a potential loop or misconfiguration) and can take protective action, such as flagging the MAC as duplicate, which is harder to reliably detect using only local data-plane MAC learning at each switch independently
options.D: EVPN prevents duplicate MACs by permanently disabling any VNI that has ever contained more than one host

questions.explanation_es: Como la alcanzabilidad MAC se anuncia y rastrea vía rutas EVPN Type-2 de BGP (con números de secuencia), el plano de control puede detectar cuando la misma MAC se está anunciando desde dos VTEPs distintos casi simultáneamente (un posible loop o mala configuración) y tomar acción protectora, como marcar la MAC como duplicada — algo más difícil de detectar de forma confiable usando solo aprendizaje de MAC en el plano de datos de cada switch de forma independiente.

questions.name: VXLAN EVPN/BUM
questions.question: Why does a VXLAN EVPN fabric commonly need a way to handle BUM traffic even though EVPN's BGP control plane already distributes known unicast MAC reachability?

options.A: BUM traffic in a VXLAN EVPN fabric is always converted to known-unicast at the ingress VTEP by first consulting the EVPN MAC table before forwarding, so no separate multicast underlay or ingress-replication mechanism is ever required regardless of fabric size
options.B: EVPN's BGP control plane specifically addresses learning and distributing known-unicast MAC-to-VTEP mappings, but broadcast, unknown-unicast, and multicast (BUM) traffic by definition must still reach multiple (or all) relevant VTEPs for a given VNI, requiring a separate mechanism (multicast underlay or ingress replication) specifically for that category of traffic, which EVPN's unicast MAC learning does not address
options.C: EVPN's BGP control plane already fully replaces the need to handle BUM traffic in any way, since all traffic becomes known-unicast automatically once EVPN is enabled
options.D: BUM traffic handling is only relevant in fabrics that do not use BGP EVPN at all, and is automatically eliminated the moment EVPN is configured

questions.explanation_es: El plano de control BGP de EVPN aborda específicamente el aprendizaje y la distribución de mapeos MAC-a-VTEP de unicast conocido, pero el tráfico broadcast, unknown-unicast y multicast (BUM) por definición debe seguir llegando a múltiples (o todos) los VTEPs relevantes para una VNI dada, requiriendo un mecanismo separado (underlay multicast o replicación por ingreso) específicamente para esa categoría de tráfico, algo que el aprendizaje de MAC unicast de EVPN no resuelve por sí solo.

questions.name: Trunking 802.1Q
questions.question: What happens on a Cisco switch trunk port if the native VLAN configured on one end does not match the native VLAN configured on the other end of the same trunk link?

options.A: Native VLAN mismatches can only occur on fiber-optic trunk links and never on copper Ethernet trunk links
options.B: The trunk port immediately and permanently shuts down with no possibility of recovery once a mismatch is detected — since Cisco switches are believed to treat a native VLAN mismatch as equivalent to a security violation similar to port security's shutdown mode, requiring a manual 'shutdown'/'no shutdown' cycle to restore the interface
options.C: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) typically detects this native VLAN mismatch and generates a warning/syslog message, since untagged frames sent by one side would otherwise be silently placed into the wrong VLAN on the other side, effectively leaking traffic between two VLANs that were never meant to be bridged together
options.D: A native VLAN mismatch only affects untagged control-plane traffic such as CDP and STP BPDUs, while regular tagged user data traffic continues to be switched correctly into the intended VLAN on both ends of the trunk

questions.explanation_es: CDP típicamente detecta este desajuste de VLAN nativa y genera una advertencia/mensaje de syslog, ya que los frames sin etiquetar enviados por un lado se colocarían silenciosamente en la VLAN incorrecta del otro lado, filtrando efectivamente tráfico entre dos VLANs que nunca debían puentearse.

questions.name: Trunking 802.1Q
questions.question: Which command is commonly used on a Cisco IOS switch to restrict which VLANs are permitted to traverse a specific 802.1Q trunk link?

options.A: 'vlan access-map', which filters traffic within a single VLAN based on Layer 3/4 criteria rather than controlling which VLAN IDs are permitted to cross the trunk link itself
options.B: 'switchport trunk allowed vlan <list>', which explicitly defines the set of VLANs permitted to be carried across that trunk, pruning all other VLANs from that particular link
options.C: 'spanning-tree vlan <list> priority', which only affects STP priority and has no effect on which VLANs are allowed across the trunk — though sometimes mistakenly believed to implicitly prune any VLAN assigned the lowest priority value
options.D: 'switchport trunk native vlan <id>', which defines the trunk's untagged native VLAN and, as a side effect, also restricts which tagged VLANs are permitted to traverse that same trunk link

questions.explanation_es: 'switchport trunk allowed vlan <lista>' define explícitamente el conjunto de VLANs permitidas para transportarse a través de ese trunk, podando todas las demás VLANs de ese enlace en particular — útil para limitar el alcance de broadcast domains y mejorar la seguridad.

questions.name: Trunking 802.1Q
questions.question: What is the difference between 'switchport mode trunk' and 'switchport mode dynamic desirable' on a Cisco switch interface?

options.A: 'switchport mode dynamic desirable' statically forces the port into trunk mode immediately upon configuration, while 'switchport mode trunk' instead waits for DTP negotiation with the far end to complete before the port begins operating as a trunk
options.B: 'switchport mode dynamic desirable' always forces the port to become an access port, never a trunk, regardless of DTP negotiation results
options.C: 'switchport mode trunk' requires DTP negotiation to succeed before the port becomes a trunk, exactly like dynamic desirable
options.D: 'switchport mode trunk' statically and unconditionally configures the port as a trunk, while 'switchport mode dynamic desirable' actively attempts to negotiate trunking with the far end via DTP, becoming a trunk only if the neighbor agrees (trunk, dynamic desirable, or dynamic auto with the neighbor initiating)

questions.explanation_es: 'switchport mode trunk' configura el puerto como trunk de forma estática e incondicional, mientras que 'switchport mode dynamic desirable' intenta activamente negociar trunking con el extremo remoto vía DTP, volviéndose trunk solo si el vecino está de acuerdo (trunk, dynamic desirable, o dynamic auto con el vecino iniciando la negociación).

questions.name: Trunking 802.1Q
questions.question: Why is it generally considered a security best practice to explicitly configure 'switchport nonegotiate' (or disable DTP) on trunk links between switches, rather than leaving DTP negotiation enabled?

options.A: 'switchport nonegotiate' has little security benefit and is recommended purely to reduce CPU load on very old switch hardware
options.B: Disabling DTP negotiation is required by 802.1Q itself and trunking is not supported without first disabling DTP
options.C: Leaving DTP negotiation enabled mainly increases CPU utilization on the switch due to periodic DTP frame processing, with the primary motivation for 'nonegotiate' being performance rather than preventing a rogue device from negotiating unauthorized trunk access
options.D: Leaving DTP negotiation enabled on a port that should always be a trunk introduces a risk that an attacker connecting a rogue device configured to negotiate trunking could potentially cause that port to become a trunk, gaining access to multiple VLANs that a simple access port would not have exposed; explicitly and statically configuring trunk mode with negotiation disabled removes that risk

questions.explanation_es: Dejar la negociación DTP habilitada en un puerto que siempre debería ser trunk introduce el riesgo de que un atacante conectando un dispositivo malicioso configurado para negociar trunking pueda hacer que ese puerto se vuelva trunk, ganando acceso a múltiples VLANs que un simple puerto de acceso no habría expuesto; configurar explícita y estáticamente el modo trunk con la negociación deshabilitada elimina ese riesgo (parte de la mitigación de ataques de VLAN hopping).

questions.name: Trunking 802.1Q
questions.question: What does the 802.1Q 'TPID' (Tag Protocol Identifier) field indicate within an Ethernet frame?

options.A: The TPID field only exists in IPv6 frames and has no equivalent or use in IPv4-carrying Ethernet frames
options.B: The TPID field contains the actual numeric VLAN ID value itself, functioning identically to the VLAN ID field
options.C: The TPID is a fixed value (0x8100 for standard 802.1Q) placed where the EtherType field would normally be, signaling to the receiving device that this frame carries an 802.1Q tag (with the VLAN ID and PCP fields following) rather than being an untagged frame
options.D: The TPID field stores the numeric VLAN ID being carried in that particular frame, functioning as the primary identifier switches use to determine which VLAN a tagged frame belongs to

questions.explanation_es: El TPID es un valor fijo (0x8100 para 802.1Q estándar) colocado donde normalmente iría el campo EtherType, señalando al dispositivo receptor que este frame lleva una etiqueta 802.1Q (con los campos de VLAN ID y PCP a continuación) en lugar de ser un frame sin etiquetar.

questions.name: Trunking 802.1Q
questions.question: How does 802.1Q tagging typically interact with the maximum frame size ('baby giant' frames) on an Ethernet link?

options.A: 802.1Q tagging is only possible on frames that are already at the absolute minimum Ethernet frame size of 64 bytes
options.B: Adding an 802.1Q tag increases the frame size by 4 bytes beyond the standard untagged Ethernet frame size, which is why many switches support slightly larger 'baby giant' frames specifically to accommodate tagged frames without exceeding what would otherwise be treated as an oversized/invalid frame
options.C: 802.1Q tagging has little effect on frame size, since the tag is inserted without consuming any additional bytes
options.D: 802.1Q tagging always reduces the frame size by 4 bytes compared to an untagged frame, the opposite of its actual effect

questions.explanation_es: Agregar una etiqueta 802.1Q aumenta el tamaño del frame en 4 bytes respecto al tamaño estándar de un frame Ethernet sin etiquetar, por eso muchos switches soportan frames 'baby giant' ligeramente más grandes específicamente para acomodar frames etiquetados sin que se traten como frames sobredimensionados/inválidos.

questions.name: Trunking 802.1Q
questions.question: In a design where an IP phone and a PC share a single switch port (phone in the middle, PC connected to the phone's own switch port), how does 802.1Q trunking commonly get used at that access-layer port?

options.A: This scenario requires the port to become a completely unrestricted 802.1Q trunk carrying every VLAN configured anywhere in the switch, with no distinction between voice and data, since the phone's internal three-port switch is assumed to require full trunk visibility to tag its own management traffic, rather than only the two specific VLAN IDs it actually needs for voice and data
options.B: The switch port is often configured as a sort of limited multi-VLAN access port (using an auxiliary/voice VLAN alongside a data VLAN), where the IP phone tags its own voice traffic with the voice VLAN ID while the PC's traffic remains untagged in the native/data VLAN — a specialized trunking-like behavior rather than a full unrestricted trunk
options.C: IP phones can never share a switch port with a PC ; each device always requires a fully separate physical cable run
options.D: The PC's traffic must always be tagged with the voice VLAN ID, identical to the phone's traffic, with no separate data VLAN involved

questions.explanation_es: El puerto suele configurarse como una especie de puerto de acceso multi-VLAN limitado (usando una VLAN auxiliar/de voz junto a una VLAN de datos), donde el teléfono IP etiqueta su propio tráfico de voz con el VLAN ID de voz mientras el tráfico del PC permanece sin etiquetar en la VLAN nativa/de datos — un comportamiento tipo trunking especializado, no un trunk completo sin restricciones.

questions.name: Trunking 802.1Q
questions.question: Which show command is commonly used on a Cisco IOS switch to verify the current trunking status, native VLAN, and allowed VLAN list of an interface?

options.A: 'show vlan brief', which lists each VLAN's assigned access ports but does not display a trunk interface's native VLAN or allowed-VLAN list directly
options.B: 'show mac address-table', which only shows learned MAC-to-port bindings and does not display trunk status directly
options.C: 'show interfaces trunk', which lists trunk interfaces along with their native VLAN, allowed VLAN list, and the VLANs currently active/forwarding on that trunk
options.D: 'show spanning-tree vlan 1', which only shows STP topology information for VLAN 1 and does not display trunk allowed-VLAN configuration

questions.explanation_es: 'show interfaces trunk' lista las interfaces trunk junto con su VLAN nativa, la lista de VLANs permitidas, y las VLANs actualmente activas/reenviando en ese trunk — el comando de verificación más directo para confirmar el estado de trunking en Cisco IOS.

questions.name: Trunking 802.1Q
